title: Planting chives
summary: A few weeks before the last frost.
steps: Plant a pot or division in a sunny spot or a 4 L (1 gal) pot.
Space clumps 25 cm (10 in) apart and water well.
Every three or four years in spring, dig the clump, split it into fist-sized pieces and replant.

title: Cutting chives
summary: Leaves all season, flowers in spring.
steps: Cut a handful of leaves 2.5 cm (1 in) above the soil; they regrow in a few weeks.
Cut the whole clump back after flowering for a fresh flush.
Chop and freeze in a bag, or in ice cube trays with a little water or oil. Dried chives lose most of their flavor.

title: Planting thyme
steps: Plant in sandy, well-drained soil or a pot with gritty mix, 30 cm (12 in) apart.
Water only until it settles in; after that, water when the soil is dry.
Trim the tips after flowering to keep it compact.

title: Harvesting and drying thyme
summary: Sprigs any time, the most just before it flowers.
steps: Snip the soft top 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 in) of the stems; never cut into the bare woody part.
Tie small bundles and hang them upside down in a warm, dry, shady place for one to two weeks.
Strip the dry leaves into a jar and keep it out of the light.

title: Planting rosemary
summary: After the last frost, from a plant.
steps: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, or in a 19 L (5 gal) pot with gritty mix.
Water deeply once a week until new growth starts, then only in long dry spells.
In places colder than its zones, keep it in a pot and move it to a bright, cool spot before hard freezes.

title: Cutting and drying rosemary
summary: Sprigs year-round once it is settled.
steps: Cut 10 to 15 cm (4 to 6 in) sprigs from the green tips, never more than a third of the plant at a time.
Hang bundles to dry, or freeze sprigs whole in a bag.
Soft tips root easily in moist mix if you want more plants.

title: Planting mint in a pot
steps: Plant a rooted piece in an 11 L (3 gal) pot with ordinary potting mix.
To grow it in a bed, sink a bottomless pot or bucket 25 cm (10 in) deep with its rim above the soil, and plant inside it.
Keep it moist. Cut it back by half in midsummer for fresh leaves.

title: Picking and drying mint
summary: Pick often to keep it leafy.
steps: Pinch or cut stem tips just above a pair of leaves; two new stems grow from there.
Pick the most just before it flowers, in the morning after the dew dries.
Dry on screens or in bundles, then crumble the leaves into jars for tea.

title: Planting sage
steps: Plant in full sun and lean, well-drained soil, 45 cm (18 in) apart.
Water until it is growing well, then let the soil dry between waterings.
In spring, cut it back by about a third to keep it bushy.

title: Harvesting and drying sage
summary: Lightly the first year, more after that.
steps: Pick single leaves or cut stem tips as you need them.
For drying, cut stems before the plant flowers and lay the leaves flat on a screen in a shady, airy spot.
Store dry leaves whole in a jar and crumble them when you cook.

title: Sowing epazote
steps: Scatter the tiny seeds on the surface and press them in; they need light to sprout.
Thin to 30 cm (12 in) apart.
Grow it in a pot or a corner where its self-sown seedlings won't become a nuisance.

title: Harvesting epazote
summary: A few leaves at a time.
steps: Pick young leaves and tips as you need them, starting about six weeks after sowing.
Add one sprig or a few leaves to a pot of beans in the last 15 minutes of cooking. More is not better.
Dry leaves in bundles for winter, and cut off flower heads to stop it seeding everywhere.

title: Planting lemongrass
steps: Root grocery-store stalks in a glass of water, changing the water every few days, until roots are 2.5 cm (1 in) long.
Plant them 60 cm (2 ft) apart in rich soil, or in a 19 L (5 gal) pot.
Water often and feed monthly; it grows fast in heat.

title: Harvesting lemongrass
summary: Stalks as thick as a pencil or more.
steps: Wearing gloves, cut or twist off outer stalks at the base when they are 1 cm (1/2 in) thick or more.
Use the pale lower part for cooking; dry or steep the green leaves for tea.
Freeze chopped stalks in bags, and before frost, divide the clump and pot a piece to bring inside.
